Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Can you provide information on the legendary Jedi, including their names and notable accomplishments?
Answer: Sure thing! I have a total of five Jedi for you. Canon: As the title may have suggested… he’s Grandmaster of the Order. Yoda was arguably the greatest lightsaber duelist to ever grace the galaxy, and immensely powerful in the Force. He was the most powerful Jedi alive for much of his life. And he was renowned for being wise. He mainly used the fourth form of lightsaber combat: Ataru. And was the greatest of all its users, although he did master all the classic forms. Yoda is also the second Jedi to learn the Force ghost ability, and he lived to be 900 years old. Mace Windu was just about as skilled as Yoda and not too far off in terms of power either. He mastered all the forms and made his own: Vaapad. It was designed to harness his aggression and be a vent for him, so he could use anger without using the Dark Side, however he could use the Dark Side… in others. Aggression from Dark Siders was redirected and used with Vaapad, making Mace a nightmare for Sith. He also is the only Canon user of Shatterpoint, an ability that reveals weak points in people and even events! If this list was based on purely skill and power, Anakin would go here, but I’m valuing a mixture of skill, power, and philosophy. Trueness to what it means to be an ideal Jedi. Qui-Gon is more ideal, but much less deadly, and Plo Koon is just a little behind in both. Obi-Wan has the most screentime of all my mentions. He is also the greatest Soresu practitioner ever (Soresu is the defensive style, form 3) Kenobi is extremely heroic and brave, but also has great street-smarts/BIQ, which allows him to survive incredibly unfavorable odds and beat stronger opponents due to mindfulness. Legends: In his Legends prime, he is Grandmaster of the new Jedi Order. And he becomes the strongest Jedi in history (strongest Force User ever debatably - not counting Force entities) And also the best in the other two categories I keep mentioning: Jedi-philosophy and lightsaber skill. He made the Order on top of the old one and learned from mistakes he didn’t have to make. Luke Skywalker in Legends is what I call the ideal Jedi. And lastly, I’ll mention my favorite: He is not the strongest or best in almost any sense, but in all he is great. Plo Koon is a master of Form V, Djem So/Shien. Like Anakin. In Legends (pretty much the only place he really exists) he beat Ventress while he had a broken arm - that is using a very two-handed form. And has plenty of feats that put him above most of if not all Canon Jedi. He also has one of the most diverse sets of abilities ever, mastering many families of Force powers. And he is so good and kind. He is brilliantly brave, contagiously caring and wooingly? wise… I tried okay, that’s what counts. Fun facts: Legends - he was said to beat Yoda in a duel and is the first Jedi to use Electric Judgment. Canon - his age is unknown, he discovered Ahsoka, and he leads the 104th batalion, A.K.A. the Wolf Pack. (In my opinion, the tightest of all clones; no Jedi loved his clones more than Plo Koon did) This Jedi Master also has only 1 organic kill as someone who fought in many wars, that’s how much he values life.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What is the age of Palpatine in Star Wars Legends (non-Canon)?
Answer: He was born in 82 BBY in Legends, and for Canon, he was born 84 BBY (which makes Canon Sidious 2 years older) Sources are “Star Wars: Timelines” for Canon and Major Character Birth Years for Legends. BBY stand for Before the Battle of Yavin. 0 BBY is the year A New Hope takes place in, so in that movie, Palpatine is 84 (Canon) or 82 (Legends) Pretty insignificant in my opinion, but fun facts are fun facts; now you know!

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why is Qui-Gon Jinn so beloved? Was he reckless and disobedient, especially to the Council?
Answer: For one, he was played by Liam Neeson. Queue the taken/Star Wars crossover memes. But for his actual character, he’s a bloody lovable guy! He is clam, caring, and patient, he even kept teaching this little sassy bugger for years: Very wise too, that’s a defining part of him. And he’s actually not reckless. The rest of the Jedi are more reckless than he is for blindly following rules above all else. Qui-Gon listened to the Force above all else. Rather than being disobedient to the Council, he was just more obedient to the Force. That’s where the disagreements came from. Which is a great reason if anything. Anakin had less reason to disobey the Council yet did it more often, and people love him! More for his wittiness and heroism, but it goes to show, at the very least, being disobedient does not take much away from likeability among Star Wars fans.

Question: How scary and dangerous would Yoda be if he fully went to the dark side?
Answer: Scarier than the Son! What’d you do if Dark Yoda was hunting you in the SW Galaxy? "At this moment, Yoda turned, and Dooku gasped. Whether it was the play of the holomonitors, beaming their views of bleak space and distant battles, or some other trick of the light, Yoda's face was deeply hidden in the shadows, and for one terrible instant, he looked exactly like Darth Sidious. Or rather, it was Yoda as he might have been, or could yet become: a Yoda gone rotten, a Yoda whose awesome powers had been utterly unleashed by his connection to the dark side… In a flash Dooku saw how foolish he had been, trying to urge the old Master to the dark side. If Yoda ever turned that way, Sidious himself would be annihilated. The universe had yet to comprehend the kind of evil that a Jedi Knight of nearly nine hundred years could wield.” - Star Wars: Dark Rendezvous Maybe it’s moot, but what seals the deal for me is that the Son is bound, Dark Side Yoda would be on the loose and ready to “unlimited power” anyone he comes across. He’d also know a great deal about the Jedi and the rest of the Galaxy in general, which only makes things worse.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Which fictional character has the most aura in appearance alone?
Answer: Appearance alone? Interesting. Without any knowledge on the characters, I honestly think Darth Vader and Superman would look a bit stupid. And Plo Koon is all about what’s on the inside, so that aura is definitely reliant on more than just appearance. So, I’d choose Batman. This guy is someone who needs no explanation for you to understand what he’s about. Just one look, and you know he’s out to beat you up. Nothing more. Now that is what I call aura. Captain America is close - I mean, his suit is basically just the American flag - but I still choose Batman over him. Cap’s about hope and perfect patriotism: making your country the best it can be, the flag alone is not enough to say that. However, this: Sends a clear message in my opinion.

Question: Why is there a lack of aliens or minorities leads in Star Wars media (TV, movies, video games)?
Answer: I have no clue. Being realistic, it’s good to have some minority/alien leads. But Star Wars somehow avoids it even with a galaxy of many races! Wouldn’t it have been great to have some spectacular female lead? Maybe an alien; she could even be the apprentice of Anakin himself and get her own spin-off! That sounds like it could be great; in fact, it would be a prime example of an alien/minority lead. I can image her as one of the most popular character in SW, maybe even as a star in the most popular SW series! We could also have had someone who’s in a cultural minority. That would be cool. Heck, we could have someone totally unique, like one female clone among millions! Oh, you know those Jedi Masters? Imagine diversity there! Star really missed an opportunity. Man, I could go on with all these possibilities, but I assume you could too, so I’ll leave it here. Boo Star Wars! Shame on them for having no diversity!

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What were the strengths of the two sides of the Force that trained Qui Gon Jinn: The Living Force and The Cosmic Force?
Answer: I think you misunderstand the relationship between the three. You could say the Force taught Qui-Gon, but it wouldn’t be that literal; rather Jinn actively studied and learned from the Force. And for the relationship of the Living and Cosmic Forces… one doesn’t really have strength over the other. Imagine you are the cosmic Force. You have a fish tank (the galaxy) and a hand (the Living Force) you put into the fish tank to interact. It’s not a perfect analogy, but I think it gets the point across. The Living Force is just a smaller bound part of the greater Force. Through the people, the Living Force resides; it is what Jedi and Sith can use. But the source is greater and beyond just time and space. It’s what the dead become a part of. And that explains why Force Ghosts can appear throughout time and space; it’s somewhat like the World between Worlds. Only, it’s not a path in between the doors, the doors are inside the Cosmic Force

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Could Obi-Wan sense Anakin's presence through the Force?
Answer: Yes. In the Kenobi series he could sense Vader (episode 3) And he only briefly felt Anakin’s presence in the Dark Side once before. Likewise, Vader could sense Obi-Wan presence even after many years of not seeing him. While I feel their complex and deep bond certainly makes it easier, I would argue any two powerful Force users could sense each other’s presence and identify one another if they’ve met.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Which character has the most satisfying arc in Star Wars: The Clone Wars and what makes it satisfying?
Answer: Ahsoka. I talk about her arc in detail here: What makes it so satisfying is that it came from a dislikable place and ended in a really amazing one. She wasn’t terrible originally, but she was snarky and wasn’t going anywhere for a while. Then she overcame narrow views, grew in skill, power and wisdom. Eventually, she played a pivotal role in the siege of Mandalore and battled Maul! Another reason it’s satisfying is how well and gradually it was done. Slow, but fast enough to feel.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Can you tell me about Yoda's past and what he did when he was younger?
Answer: His past is mostly a mystery, but some stories of his have been shared over the years. Many taking place before The Phantom Menace. Like some shown in flashbacks in the Canon Yoda comics. Many years before, Yoda helped end a conflict between primitive peoples. He stopped raids and inspired friendship between the two sides, by shedding light on how both had their own major disadvantages. He even inspired a young native called Bree to be better, whom Yoda came back to years later. The comics have solid art and overall top quality. I highly recommend it.

Question: Does Anakin's voice sound different in 'The Clone Wars' compared to the movies?
Answer: Because it is a different voice! Hayden Christensen plays Anakin Skywalker in Attack of the Clones and Revenge of the Sith. But in the Clone Wars, Anakin is voice-acted by Matt Lanter. Question: Is it worth watching Star Wars? I’ve never seen a single movie.
Answer: Absolutely. >>This answer is for the people who have not seen Star Wars<< I won’t be using how much I love some projects or the “quality” as part of the following. If you like comics, Star Wars has hundreds! If you like more deep classics, the OT will serve you well. If you like… I think you get it. Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What lessons can we learn from Qui-Gon Jinn that can be applied to everyday life?
Answer: My number one pick is here: So many of us focus on the scary things, the overwhelming things and pains tomorrow might have in store. But what does that actually help? Remember you have something to do right now. Be mindful of the future, but not at the expense of the moment. What happens now changes the future. And being focused is so undervalued. It gives peace and makes you a damn formidable force. And that’s my second pick right there. Do good simply because it is good. Not for a future reward, and definitely not to look good or feel good about yourself. Then you’re making it about yourself. Do good…

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why is Emperor Palpatine called "Darth" in all Star Wars media, even though his name was not originally Darth before becoming a Sith?
Answer: His name was not Darth before being a Sith because “Darth” is a Sith title! It’s actually a compressed version of “Dark Lord of the Sith” That also explains why there are so many Darths. Something related is the name that comes after Darth is also no original name. It’s normally related to a word fitting for the character. Count Dooku became Darth Tyranus (relating to tyrant) Anakin Skywalker became Darth Vader (Dutch word for “father”) Sheev Palpatine became Darth Sidious (derived from insidious, which means ”proceeding in a gradual, subtle way, but with very harmful effects) Which is poetic genius in my mind.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What are your top 5 favorite Star Wars lightsaber battles?
Answer: #5 Ahsoka Tano vs Maul It’s either this or Obi-Wan and Anakin vs Dooku during the Sifo-Dyas arc. Both were done so well, but this was TCW’s animation on overdrive and it was done by motion capture with Ray Park!! The OG The footwork was especially good, and it was two fan-favorites fighting, who wouldn’t love it? #4 Luke Skywalker vs Darth Vader (RotJ) While the choreography wasn’t so flashy, the weight of this duel was incredible. And the moment of Anakin’s redemption is what I like to call “the moment of Star Wars” All in all, it’s just very nostalgic and emotional. #3 Old Ben vs Maul This one is the shortest duel on the list, but the most poetic. The break down is incredible and each stance has meaning (the stances also make up most of the fight) It’s just so well executed, even the music tells a story. And this is also an end to the epic rivalry between Maul and Obi-Wan. #2 Obi-Wan Kenobi vs The Brothers As a Kenobi fan, I love this. Simply because it’s such an epic feat and pushed Obi-Wan’s Soresu to its limit. Also, a fun detail from it is that there is a direct parallel between him and Adi-Gallia. They both kicked Savage’s leg, and it did nothing, but while Gallia was frightened and froze to get rammed, Kenobi stayed fast and continued bravely, kept chipping until it crippled. #1 Obi-Wan Kenobi vs Knightfall Vader… what else? All art was by “Venamis” This did not need much meaning. It’s the longest duel ever (longest “sword” duel in movie history) And just incredible overall. So fast and flashy. That’s not even all of it; it’s also super emotional (I’d argue at least second most) I don’t know what else to say; it was long and hard fought, it had excellent moves and footwork. It is a fan-favorite for good reason.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why did Yoda think that redemption from the Dark Side was not possible?
Answer: Given his experience, it makes sense. Jedi barely ever see redemption from the Dark Side. Yoda’s seen first-hand how hopeless the situation can be. His old Padawan Dooku left and refused to come back. All Yoda has seen of the Dark Side’s temptation was its effectiveness and grip. Plus, Yoda was pretty stuck in his ways during the Prequels; it’s likely he was just sure of this without any proof and didn’t give it much further thought. To be fair, it is highly unlikely. We as fans can name a good amount of redeemed Dark Siders, but in-universe almost all of them stay on the Dark Side once they get on it.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Was Yoda right that fear leads to anger, anger leads to hate, and hate leads to suffering? Why or why not?
Answer: I personally believe he was right. Actually, I think what he says happens most of the time one of those negativities is involved. Think about a real and common example. Imagine you friend is scared of losing his treasure or his safety. Unless he’s under paralyzing fear, he’ll be angry. And anger leading to hate is rather obvious. Insults turn into fights, and there is never a true winner in a heated fight, only one who walked away with less loss. And on a large scale this is more true. Fear makes people go crazy with anger. Those who don’t fear as much see others as paranoid while the scared see the others as foolish. Anger does lead to hate and that always leads to suffering. Emotionally or physically if it escalates to fighting and warring.

Question: Was Luke discovering the charred remains of his uncle and aunt, the catalyst that drove him to become a Jedi?
Answer: It was the point of no return. It’s ironically not included in the infographic - because it’s not as common as the others. But anyway, the point of no return comes after the “meeting with the mentor”, or reluctant acceptance of the call. Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How did Dooku beat Obi-wan so easily but lose to Anakin who lost to Obi-Wan?
Answer: A few factors play into this. Makashi is excellent for taking out Obi-Wan’s defense. A friend of mine made this analogy: Obi-Wan’s Soresu is like a lock; smashing it with Djem So won’t work, however, picking it carefully will. And Makashi’s elegance pretty much fades away when faced with Djem So. Anakin’s attacks are like waves, you don’t just redirect them. The one-handed form of Makashi stands little chance against the greatest Djem So the galaxy has yet seen. In both fights these are important. Obi-Wan was in his peak at Mustafar and was completely focused because he had to be. Dooku was meant to target Kenobi first and not meant to kill Anakin (I don't think he would have won without Palpatine’s restrictions, but I think it had an effect) And Anakin severely overestimated his abilities in the Mustafar duel. This is very similar to some of the mindsets mentioned above. In the first duel, Anakin tapped into his anger and used the Dark Side to become faster and stronger. No down sides that effect the duel. On Mustafar, the downsides came into play. He was grossly overconfident and less mindful. Skywalker was focused, but not like he was back in the days he was a general. He was only focused on winning, not outside factors like the all-important and famous highground!

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Which Star Wars characters are perfect representations of their factions?
Answer: I have two complimentary picks. Darth Maul - Sith Apprentice Palpatine or Darth Vader probably come first to your mind when you think Sith, but Maul sticks to firmly to the Sith ideology, the only thing stopping him from being the perfect Sith - in my mind - is the fact that he was never truly in charge. Hence why I’m listing him specifically as an apprentice. Darth Maul was “taught” cruelly by Palpatine since childhood and knew only rage and hate. He was a step behind his master, but still very cunning and on a blood thirsty quest for power and revenge. Pure rage and fixation on something that ultimately will not matter. Obi-Wan - Jedi Master Art by Simone Ragazzoni Obi-Wan was totally dedicated to the rules, but unlike Mace Windu, Kenobi’s heart lay within the rules too. He naturally was inclined to follow them. Obi-Wan simply wanted to be given a good task and then carry it out nobly. He wants to serve and protect however he can, and that was at the core of the Jedi Order. This Jedi Master is one of the very few who could operate heroically under the politics and complications of the Order. He’s the ultimate example of what the Jedi in the Order should have been. Jedi overall should be like Qui-Gon and Luke.

Question: Does Spider-Man actually die in Infinity War or not because he’s alive in Far From Home, yet it came out a year later?
Answer: Peter Parker does get dusted away in Infinity War. The reason he’s alive again is because the Avengers reversed the effects of Thanos’ blip. Specifically, Banner Hulk snapped everyone who died back to life in Endgame. Far from Home comes after Endgame. As you can probably tell, Stark died before Far From Home. Tony’s death is part of FFH’s plot after all, and it happened in Endgame.

Question: Which force lightning is stronger, normal force lightning, purple force lightning (from Starkiller), or red force lightning?
Answer: None! Color is irrelevant to actual power. Darth Tenebrous had red lightning but he was far inferior to Palpatine. Yet the Son, an embodiment of the Dark Side most likely stronger than Palpatine, also had red lightning. And wherever you place Dooku among the above, that should make a solid inconsistency.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Who would win in a duel: Darth Maul or Mace Windu?
Answer: Mace Windu. Maul is very impressive. He’s a fantastic duelist and has better feats than Mace in terms of raw Force power. But in terms of dueling, Windu makes up for that. While how much better ether is at their specialty is debatable, something objective is that Mace Windu has a massive advantage thanks to his specific form. Vaapad thrives off of aggression (specifically aggression from the opponent) and Maul uses the most vicious form of the classic 7 - Juyo. Which is ironically the foundation for Vaapad. Considering this, I am pretty sure mace Windu would win.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Do you think "Star Wars: Skeleton Crew" will succeed in getting Star Wars out of its Skywalker-centric safe zone?
Answer: I must say I’m confident in saying no. The Acolyte explored a time far from the Skywalker Saga, that didn’t “get Star Wars out of it”. And it would honestly be very hard to separate Star Wars from being Skywalker-centric. Because that’s what Star Wars is!!! The Star Wars story revolves around the fulfillment of the prophecy. It all comes from that, so to make Star Wars revolve around something else is to destroy and remake Star Wars. Even the Skeleton Crew won’t be truly separate from the Skywalkers. It can just branch far out like Andor. All the SW roads lead to the Skywalker story. And to be honest, having something Skywalker-centric is not automatically safe. It actually readies fans to be angry about how bad you messed it up.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Are there any characters in Star Wars who do not use a lightsaber?
Answer: Pretty much every non-Force-Sensitive, but some Sith and Jedi too. The most notable example is Palpatine. He was so powerful in the Original Trilogy he finally surpassed the need for a lightsaber. He believed Sith only needed the Dark Side as a weapon, and eventually it was true for him. But why wasn’t it before? Well, Force Shields. Force Attacks won’t always work if your opponent in concentrated and relative to your strength. A lightsaber is very effective and makes thing much easier, and with everyone else using them, it’s hard to keep up without one. But there’s one less powerful Jedi we don’t talk much about: Bruu Jun-Fan Obviously, he does use a lightsaber. He doesn't perfectly fit the bill, but Force Augmentation is his primary weapon, while his lightsaber is secondary - that’s my take.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: If baby Yoda is the age of a middle-aged human, why does he have the maturity of a baby?
Answer: Because he is a baby. Grogu is not a human. He is part a mysterious unnamed species we know little about. But one thing we do know is that Yoda - a member of the same species - lived to 900. Grogu is 50, one eighteenth of that age. Proportionally, he’s 5 (Dividing 100 by 18; if we dived the average human male lifespan - 70 years - by that same number, baby Yoda here is the equivalent of 4)

Question: Who is your favorite clone in Star Wars (excluding ARC Troopers)? What makes them your favorite and do you have any unpopular opinions about them?
Answer: Tech. My unpopular opinion is that he was not great for a lot of the start. No depth. A typical brainy character by itself is just an entertaining side that helps the team. He was not lead material. I love the smart characters with Artemis Fowl and Tony Stark, but only when they’re well written and have things outside of smarts. I truly loved him after this moment: He bravely dives in to save Omega without thought and has a great conversation with her. Tech tells her how just because he goes through his emotions differently and expresses his feelings in a dissimilar way doesn’t mean he doesn’t have those emotions and feelings. And that’s what I love about him. The actual complexity he had after some good writing. I can relate to that. All INTJs - and similar personality types - can. When I can feel like I’m in the story through a character, that’s when I’m most enjoying it.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What are the three major factions in Star Wars and what are their goals and levels of power?
Answer: There are three major factions that stay in the game. Throughout Star Wars history, you will likely find all of these. You could substitute this for Mandalorians only to get a more powerful faction overall and an extra goal (in Legends, they had big dreams and fought a full-on war with the Jedi) But that costs “major-ness”, as Mandalorians are more rare. Their goal is quite simple: attain fame and money. (sometimes they just want fame for more money) The Jedi Order is often the most powerful group not by average, but by number. Jedi Knights are legendary throughout the galaxy and the Order has thousands of them. The Jedi Order’s goal is to maintain and bring peace, although they are often caught slacking by fans. Their goals are completely self-centered. Me, me, me, I, I, I. Whether that means ruling the galaxy or making someone suffer. On average, the Sith are arguably the most powerful of these factions. Especially while the Rule of Two is working.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why has Darth Maul become so popular among Star Wars fans? He is a character without personality, he never speaks and says 2 phrases in the entire film.
Answer: Well, TPM Maul was popular because… come on, it’s a double lightsaber! He’s just cool. And that’s really all it takes to be liked by fans sometimes. I don’t think that’s bad, honestly. But his real popularity comes from the Clone Wars series. He speaks often there, and Sam Writer does fantastic voice acting. In the show, he has depth, and it shows you his perspective. Maul makes a great comeback and arcs that follow him are spectacular. He just adds so much great content. His arc overall and specifically its end in Rebels is pretty darn great in my opinion. And personally, I think he is the best embodiment of the “Sith Apprentice” in the Star Wars Canon.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: If the Clone Wars from "Star Wars" were real, which side would you choose to join and why?
Answer: The Republic for two reasons. 1 while the Republic isn’t full of saints, the CIS is full-on a terrorist group. They are the bad guys, I’m sorry, but it’s true. Sepratist people are victims, but they ultimately support evil. 2 it would be a better life. What started the war (on the surface) was the neglect of Outer Rim worlds. They have resources exported to the Core and have terrible law enforcement; overall, they get the cons of being part of the Republic, but none of the pros. Basically, in the CIS you’d be paying loads of taxes thanks to the war and that’s about it. In the Galactic Republic, you’d still be paying, but you’d be in a much more prosperous area and business opportunities would be better. But if you wanted to avoid the war all together, it would be easier to slip away under the Separatists.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What are some underutilized force powers in Star Wars that could be very powerful if used more frequently?
Answer: For a generic pick: Force Speed. Jedi can use a draining power to move at incredible speeds. While it’s not always a good idea in combat, it is definitely underutilized and has its would-be moments in duels. We saw it once, and never again in the Canon. They could be zipping around like the Flash, blurring around, but no. For more unique picks… I have three. All ones Plo Koon knew in Legends. On its highest level, the ability could tear apart armies. Users could make storms and summon lightning at will. But even on a basic level, it could be used to freeze water and summon mist for cover. Since it’s a Canon ability already, I’m disappointed in it being underutilized. I don’t know who would not want this in the Canon. The ability is very, very rare but also powerful and giving it to Plo Koon would give him some much needed Canon love. It’s almost the polar opposite of Force Scream. This ability can transfer thoughts and images to teammates and boosts synergy tremendously. It can also demoralize enemies. I really love the ability and wish it was used in the Canon.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why do Jedi bother using light sabers? Why don't they just force choke each other and the most powerful one wins?
Answer: Force Shields. Oversimplified, the Force Shield ability just makes you immune to Force attacks. As long as your opponent isn’t much stronger than you. And that’s a thing because fights would be very unentertaining if they didn’t exist. It would be about who Force Chokes first. So instead of getting this: We’d get a quick neck break. Maybe even ties. Imagine how lame it would be to have some random Padawan get the drop on Vader. So, in the SW universe, the answer is Force Shields. In our world, it’s “because that would look lame.”

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What MCU villain can you sympathize with?
Answer: Loki. Maybe it’s all because of Hiddleston’s hypnotizing performance. But honestly, he was broken. I’m not saying his actions were justified (no true villain had really justifiable actions, just understandable ones) He lived in his brother's shadow, and no one noticed. And he was lied to about his true father for decades. In the Dark World you really start to sympathize with him. Then we see he’s more human than we thought. And there he loses the only one who could actually see him. To everyone else, he was Thor’s shadow. And it’s not simply being looked down on that made him evil. He just wanted to be equals with his brother, that’s all. But he was pushed aside and later he discovered he wasn’t even an Odinson really. He was a “fake” just like everyone treated him as. It becomes very understandable that he grew up wanting to rule. He was always denied, so he started wanting to be the one in charge and deny others.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Is the strength of Siths greater than that of Jedi due to their connection with the dark side of the Force?
Answer: Yes, in Canon, the average Sith is stronger than the average Jedi. It is not, however, due to the Dark Side. The main reason is that the Sith are all about power. While the Jedi are focused on “protecting the galaxy.” The way these two go about doing things leads to a difference in power. And the numbers are the second most impactful factor. Imagine it’s about schooling. The Sith are like Greek philosophers who focus on a single student. The teacher teaches all he knows and discovers more until his apprentice becomes a master, and the cycle continues. That’s the genius of Darth bane But the Jedi are like a normal school system. A few teachers, loads of students. Each student ends up with a good education, but if any student gets on the same level as a Sith apprentice, it’s no thanks to the Jedi system.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: In the Star Wars universe, why is it difficult for people to understand and use "The Force"? Is it accessible to everyone?
Answer: Not everyone knows it exists. It’s something most people in Star Wars never feel, and things outside of one’s experiences are hard to understand. You need to a have a high Midi-Chlorian count to feel the Force and use it before much training. So, it’s not as well-known as one might assume and it’s also very hard for most people to use it. But there is actually a case of a non-Force Sensitives becoming Force-Sensitive in the Canon. It’s controversial, but it is Canon. Sabine Wren became Force Sensitive through training. And she confirmed it is assessable to everyone. That I actually really love. Sabine being the one specifically… not so much; she was better without it. The whole situation is perfect to me, but how it was established was objectively sub-par.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What languages do C-3PO and R2-D2 speak in Star Wars? Do they have a specific dialect or accent?
Answer: Artoo spoke Binary, a simple language comprised of two types of sounds. He was stuck to that language, it’s the only one he is capable of. C3-P0 is like the opposite. He is a protocol droid fluent in millions of languages. C3-P0 has an accent of sorts because he keeps the typical “robot assistant voice” regardless of the language he is speaking, but Artoo does not. R2-D2 has a barely unique version of Binary, so you could say he does, but I do not consider it an accent.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Is it possible to heal a red Kyber crystal, and how is that done?
Answer: This is possible! Ahsoka’s famous white lightsabers come from the process (known as “purifying” a bleed Kyber crystal) She took the crystals of an Inquisitor’s weapon to make her own. It can turn the crystal white, or to its original color. As for how it’s done, we have nothing specific yet. We can only assume it's by focusing on one’s own peace or something else opposite to channeling rage.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Was Ahsoka Tano ever promoted to the rank of Master within the Republic's ranks after her battle with Vader on Malachor in the Star Wars Canon?
Answer: Okay, there are three problems here. Order 66 wiped out the Jedi Order and its ranks lost meaning alongside the Order’s death. So, Ahsoka gaining the rank of Master for that is impossible times 3 But if we look past all that and also pretend the question “should she have been promoted for surviving a fight against Vader?”, then I’m on the fence. The prowess displayed is certainly Master-level, but combat is not what makes a Jedi Master; wisdom is more important in terms of getting the rank. Although Ahsoka has shown a lot of all the classic qualities in a Master by the time of Rebels, so I’d say the fight very well could have been the final blow to whatever was stopping the Jedi from making her a Master in this hypothetical. On the other hand, she did proudly state how she was not a Jedi, so maybe not.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What was the relationship between Dooku and Yoda?
Answer: Quite complex. Yoda was the Grand Master of the Jedi Order. Arguably its most powerful, skilled and popular member. Dooku was one of Yoda’s many apprentices. But Dooku stood out among the rest. He was second to Yoda in terms of dueling and he wasn't a slouch in knowledge of the Force either. That’s a big part of their relationship. Dooku lives in Yoda’s shadow (a bit) but seems like he has the potential to rise above his master. But the main part of their relationship’s arc to me is how Dooku went away from Yoda. Count Dooku left and became Darth Tryanus not too long after separating from Yoda. I think the defining part of this move was how Dooku thought he knew better than Yoda. The main part of their relationship is the dynamic of that and how Yoda knows Dooku thinks he’s superior in some ways. Honestly, Dooku did see past the wool over the Jedi’s eyes, but likewise, Yoda saw things that Dooku didn’t. “I am more powerful than any Jedi, even you.” “Much to learn, you still have” Those quotes imply a lot of their relationship in my mind.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How does Star Wars exist in the MCU?
Answer: An Easter Egg. In MARVEL’s “What If…” the Watcher and Infinity Ultron fight and shatter barriers of the multiverse. They fly through many different universes, and for a short few frames, the background is Mustafar. I don’t consider this Canon to either franchise, I just think of it as a fun Easter Egg. But what do you think of it?

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Was Dooku a member of the Jedi Council or just an advisor to Yoda?
Answer: Neither. Dooku was a Jedi Master, but he never made it on the Council. And Yoda was Dooku’s mentor, so if anyone was an adviser, it was Yoda. Dooku was Yoda’s most famous Padawan and highly, highly respected though. Even if his lightsaber design and focus on dueling seemed a little off to some Jedi - including Yoda - Dooku was very respected and was probably just as famous as many Masters on the Council.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What is the definition of Padawan?
Answer: One of the lower ranks for Jedi. Padawan is the second lowest rank. It is for those who are assigned to learn under a Jedi Knight or Jedi Master. Padawans collect experience and are taught by their masters over many missions and sometimes years. But Padawans get promoted by passing special trials, and if a master does not want their Padawan to take those trials, the Padawan can be held at his/her current rank for decades! (Doesn’t happen often or actually for decades, but Obi-Wan is an example of Padawans being held back for a while)

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Who is more intimidating between General Grievous and Darth Maul?
Answer: Maul is more formidable, but Grievous is undeniably more intimidating. He bakes it into his tactics. Look at that. People see aliens all the time in Star Wars. Sure, Maul doesn’t look friendly, but Grievous… He doesn’t seem like a different species; he looks like a monster. This behemoth is above 7 feet tall and will stare down at you as he talks about the new addition to his collection that’s coming soon. And he has four clawed arms to flex! On top of that, he moves like a monster. This guy is famous for Jedi hunting, he has a reputation to make you scared. Even though Maul might be more deadly, he lives in the shadows. Grievous puts himself at the front and wants everyone to know he’s the best Jedi-hunter out there.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What are the reasons for people comparing Marvel to Star Wars, even though they are two different universes with distinct storylines?
Answer: They’re both popular. A miserably one-sided fight People will compare anything and everything, especially in terms of fiction. Often, it’s just arguing and trying to prove one thing is better than the other, but I personally have more positive experiences comparing SW and MARVEL (for an example) I am a big fan of both, and when you have two people that don’t care which is better or even think one is objectively better, you are most likely going to have a great conversation. I’m not sure most people get the same experience as I do - in fact I lean towards thinking most people have more negative debates on these things - so I’ll leave with a small change that makes a big difference: remember it takes 2 to argue. Don’t feel bad to block if not replying isn’t enough to end a conversation. And focus on the positives more than the negatives!

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Does Yoda's quote "Do or do not. There is no try" mean that trying is worthless or that you should aim to succeed?
Answer: In a way, both. He said it to Luke because confidence was a key factor in what Skywalker aimed to do. How was he going to lift the X-Wing while thinking it’s impossible? In that way, he means aim to succeed. But in the way I took it, he pretty much does mean trying is worthless. That is, in the context of “do or do not”. Failure is already an option and a thing, saying “I tried” changes nothing. Yoda is about “yes” or “no” there, not “no, but…” The rest just doesn’t matter to him. If it’s a “no”, simply pick yourself up and try again later; if it’s a yes, nice job.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why does Anakin do better against Dooku by himself?
Answer: He does not, the duo just does a lot worse than you’d expect because Dooku is a dueling genius. He puts Anakin on defense and leaves Kenobi on offense. Just look at that! Anakin is being rushed back and Kenobi is barely attacking at all. Skywalker and Dooku are fighting somewhat normally while Obi-Wan attacks every now and then with sub-par offense. That’s why it’s similar to Dooku and Anakin fighting alone. Kenobi becomes something of a nonfactor when he’s forced to attack and cannot use his defense. But Anakin does not do better on his own. One would just except Kenobi to do more. Dooku lets Anakin off easy because he’s important to Sidious; if he was going all out back in The Clone Wars 2008, Anakin would have died. Anakin proved to be capable of defeating the Count in RotS, but prior, he proved he couldn't. With Obi-Wan’s help they failed, and Kenobi is very obviously adding something to the team, even if it’s little. If for some reason his attacks that threaten Dooku and force his attention away from Anakin were helping Tyranus, Kenobi would simply stad back.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Did Obi-wan tap into the Dark Side when he was fighting Darth Maul in The Phantom Menace?
Answer: He did not! So many people are confident saying he did, but they forget anger is not the Dark Side by itself, anger can be a path to it. Think about Mace Windu: he uses his anger while using the Light Side (some argue he taps into the Dark Side, but it’s more of him just being unorthodox and how Vaapad thrives with Dark Sider opponents) And Obi-Wan was not fighting with his aggression, he contained it and fought with focus: He felt anger, and gave him focus, but he did not fight with it purely, he did not let it control him. Watch closely, and you’ll see he’s fighting far too defensively to be using the Dark Side. He waits for Maul to strike and that’s not even because of his form; Obi-Wan practiced Ataru by this time, he switched to Soresu only after this duel.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Should I watch The Clone Wars to understand the Star Wars universe?
Answer: If you’re watching to understand the SW universe, TCW is the best show for you by a long shot! The Bad Batch is next in line in my opinion (it shows you the bridge between Episode 3 and 4 Most of George’s worldbuilding went to the prequel era, and there was too much to fit in to just 3 films. So, the Clone Wars was made to compliment the prequels and Filoni had many episodes to just do what he wanted. There were many fillers, but this is the case where they’re actually good; those fillers always add to the worldbuilding and add some lore. At the start, sharing lore of the SW universe is pretty much all it does, but it gets better and better with each season. Honestly, you’re in the dark among SW fans if you have not watched this show. There are many very important things in the show.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Could Anakin Skywalker understand R2-D2?
Answer: Yes, he indeed could. R2-D2 speaks what’s simply called “Binary” (like how English is called “Basic” in Star Wars, not much effort) It is also called Droidspeak, because it’s what almost every Astromech speaks. It’s made of just two main sounds, boops and beeps (okay, more like whistles and beebs) Anakin often responded to Artoo throughout the movies and series, and even as a boy he knew a few languages. So, it’s pretty clear he could in fact understand R2-D2 Fun fact: R2-D2 was a gift to Anakin from Padme; he was actually hers, she just decides to give Artoo away when she saw Anakin liked the droid.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What are some of the most perfect castings in Star Wars' history?
Answer: Ok, I’m going for obscure picks only again. Hopefully straight answers from me don’t become obscure themselves eventually. I have three picks: Pedro Pascal as Din Djarin His performance is pretty much perfect! So much emotion from under the helmet; not just any actor can convey feelings that well from behind a mask. And Din is a complex character that’s ruthless at times. With the acting handicap, so to speak, it is extremely impressive that he portrays so much so well. Sure, there could be an actor better suited to play Din, but I have not seen him. Hayden Christiansen as Anakin Skywalker (hear me out) Yeah, Anakin had choppy lines and what not, but he made Anakin. He played him quite well and the main reason he was the perfect pick is not actually his acting, it’s who he is off-screen. He is a light to everyone around him and brings smiles everywhere. The fans adore this guy! I love the guy! And actors like that, ones that fans line up to see talk, are great for the franchise. In terms of marketing specifically. Sam Writer as Starkiller Maul too. His voice acting is beyond great (he also played the Son, the Grand Inquisitor, and many more characters) But this guy is perfect because he was a fan before he was hired. And he was no casual, this man is a freaking expert. Let me just share his story of how he was hired: He was doing the motion capture for Starkiller meditating, and in the take he was very tense, flexing, balling his fists. And they asked him why, and he explains Starkiller was never on the Light Side, he never meditated, he only knows bending the Force to his will, not letting it flow. That landed him the job. He knows so much and is so mindful of almost the entire SW Canon. Sam also made the Sith Code Canon all by himself by adding it into Maul’s crazed speech. And he looks so deep and understands scenes really well; I highly recommend searching for Just see how he remembers that names of everyone and is so kind, so you can get a feel for why he’s great for SW Pedro plays Djarin perfectly Hayden is the Tom Holland of Star Wars Sam is somewhat of a mix and is so well equipped to play any part of Star Wars simply because he’s got the knowledge to correct Filoni.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What are the reasons for the dislike of the Star Wars prequels? Is it due to plot holes, George Lucas' directing, or other factors?
Answer: George Lucas' directing for the most part. People wanted a classic hero journey, like what the OT had. And then there is the dialogue. (Which I really think is not much worse than the OT’s dialogue) The last point is the CGI; people do not like the “overuse” of it. Although movies may not have been what they are today without George’s advancements in the field. What I think is the main reason that the Prequels are hated is that George wanted them to build on Star Wars, not be another standalone successful story. He made the Jedi Order, shed light on more factions, made the coolest armies in SW and added many more pieces of world-building that make the SW galaxy so interesting. Ask any fan for their favorite era, and it’s most likely going to be the Clone War era, regardless of their thoughts on Episodes 1–2 And people misunderstand Lucas felt the need to make more movies: people misunderstood Darth Vader. He was a tragic hero, not just a villain he turned good. People didn’t truly see the “hero of the Clone Wars” Old Ben mentioned Luke’s father was. And George just had so many ideas. That he had trouble remember what the audience didn't know. TCW had to fill in the gaps because three movies were not enough. Ultimately, the Prequels are very flawed, but I love them, and I know a massive chunk of the fandom does too.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Who would win: Plo Koon or Kit Fisto?
Answer: Plo Koon, whichever canon you use. In the current Canon, Kit Fisto’s best feat is fending off Grievous in TCW Not fully beating Grievous; Kit did choose to run instead of beating the leader of the droid army. He’s great, and consistently fights with the best, but in much less screentime Plo Koon has managed to show feats just as impressive as Kit’s (at the least) Plo Koon easily defeated Sing. And he could tear apart Droch-class Pod Hunter (yes, that is the correct and real name for it) with a simple Force Push after using a few Force abilities before. And he could hold a huge part of a ship from falling for almost 30 seconds: With Ahsoka, but still; Anakin and Mace Windu could not lift what was on top of them there. And in Legends, I think one feat alone puts Koon above Fisto: With a broken arm - as a Djem So practitioner - Plo easily beat Ventress. While Kit, without any handicap, lost to Asajj: Now, finally, Kit drew his lightsaber. Ventress drew a pair of blazing, red blades. She inclined her head, breathing more quickly, lips curling into a smile. "Finally," she said. "Your pleasure," Kit hissed, and went at her. He was like fire, Ventress like smoke. The dance had substance but not form, a blur of light that seemed impossibly fast, unbelievably deadly. The two leapt and swerved, collided and bounced away. Single against double light-blades. Hands, knees, feet, all in a mind-numbing blur. Obi-Wan would have given his right hand to join. Or even to watch such a display. But he had his own worries, his own battle to fight. He struggled with the urge to simply draw his lightsaber and slaughter the X'Ting. His enemies came on and on, struck quickly but clumsily, got in each other's way. Obi-Wan was direct in attack, and as elusive as a breeze. He'd missed the engagement, but suddenly — Kit was down! Wounded and groggy from a kick in the jaw, for the first time Ventress had pierced his guard. Her left-hand saber sliced his arm but as sparks flew he dove away from her left blade, leaning into a glancing blow from her right. Obi-Wan heard the scream but couldn't see the wound's severity. Kit rolled as Ventress came at him, splashing down into the lake. Ventress stood on the dock smiling hugely, arms and legs spread in triumph, laughing in that arctic voice. -The Cestus Deception I think that combination puts Plo firmly above Fisto. He also has one of the most diverse skill sets in the Jedi Order, with great practice in Alter Environment (something that could be very useful in a fight against Kit) Plo Koon uses a better Form, he’s a greater duelist overall, and his Force power is stunningly above Kit’s in both Canon and Legends. Respect the leader of the Wolf Pack!

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How does distance affect the force?
Answer: Less than you may already think. A cross-galactic Force Choke There have been feats of Sith throwing around victims from lightyears away. What really matters is whether or not you can focus on whatever you want to use the Force on. For many Jedi, it is hard to move objects when not looking at them or facing their direction. But we do see Jedi use the Force from a pretty close range most of the time, so I assume distance matters a bit, but the increase in difficulty to increase in distance is not proportional.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Are there any materials that resist lightsabers more effectively than cortosis?
Answer: No. Beskar, along with some other metals, is much stronger than Cortosis, but not better at combating a lightsaber-wielding opponent. You maybe be thinking “how does that make sense?” Well, see the power of Cortosis for yourself: A lightsaber cannot cut Cortosis because the lightsaber deactivates on contact. Not just that, but the user won’t be able to reactivate the lightsaber for a long time (in terms of combat) All of them have little chance of being cut or melted by a lightsaber, but one provides a lot more than just resistance and is theoretically impossible to cut with a lightsaber.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Do you think Anakin was a good master to Ahsoka?
Answer: Oh, absolutely; he was the perfect master for her. First of all, he trained her for the time. To survive. What’s the point of teaching her something else if that lesson would die with her shortly? And dang, he did good. Skywalker trained Ahsoka to survive anything, so she could protect herself and others. A specific case is with her Order 66 training. And on the broader side of things, let’s see some feats she achieved thanks to her training: That’s just a little. He even taught her basic practical skills like engineering. Other than that, the leaning was timed perfectly. Ahsoka came to Anakin at a time where Anakin himself still needed to develop personally. And that was a fantastic guide for Tano. That is on top of the fact that they are extremely alike! Anakin saw himself in Ahsoka, and that helped them both a lot. The cherry on top is that they were not just a great mentor-trainee pair, they were great friends.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: When Obi-wan and Anakin were dueling on Mustafar, and Obi-Wan said "it's over, I have the high ground, why didnt Vader just force choke him rather than make a stupid and daring jump that obviously didn't work out?
Answer: Partly, because of the same reason Kenobi didn’t just push Anakin in lava. Force Shields, baby! Imagine if no one could resist Force attacks regardless of their own Force power. Every fight would just be a mess of Force powers, and low level Padawans could do some serious damage to Yoda! Force Shields protect Force Sensitives from Force attacks, and that’s why Jedi use lightsabers most of the time. Now, it’s not a broken ability, it’s balanced. As long as you’re within the same league as your opponent, you can block their attacks with a Force Shield. And Anakin was not far enough above Kenobi to break his shield as he was focused. They were close enough. And thanks to the Dark Side amplifying Anakin’s impulsiveness, he made a terrible decision.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How powerful is Yoda with The Force? Did he sense Anakin's fall to the dark side?
Answer: Extremely powerful. Behold: That’s the power of Yoda In terms of the Force, he’s arguably the strongest Jedi in his time. Probably top 3 Canon Force Users ever. As for sensing Anakin’s fall… he did not. However, the Force barely gives insight to anyone when it comes to these sorts of future events. The future is always in motion and is not set in the Star Wars universe. So, he could only see some of the signs of Anakin’s fall. Yoda was unaware of Palpatine’s manipulations to Anakin and the whole Jedi Order because he was so focused on destroying and finding the illusive Sith Lord.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Does Obi-Wan Kenobi have any real character flaws?
Answer: Yes, and he’s never perfect. I know why you ask; he’s stayed kind and strong in the face of so much loss, how? And in every situation, he acts so well. But that was not always the case, Obi-Wan made many mistakes and in the end, he does think Vader is irredeemable, so we see even in his arc’s end he is not perfect. However, I could see Kenobi as having no “real” character flaws, because I look at it like this: Imagine people have characteristics on a scale of 10 to -10. So, while a person like Anakin has stats like this: (This is a quick example, excuse imperfection) Good intention: 9/10 Bravery: 10/10 Emotional control: -2/10 That negative is a big character flaw. Kenobi doesn’t have a huge weakness like that in his development. He matures and rounds out very well. So, while he’s far off from having tens all the way, he doesn't have a negative. And that’s the way I think development is meant to go. Personal weaknesses are not meant to stay part of you, they are levels you should pass eventually.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How can Star Wars fans not realize the stupidity of Emperor Palpatine substituting the clone troopers for inept storm troopers?
Answer: Oh, they realize a lot more than you think. Almost anyone I’ve seen with a take on this has had one of these stances on the topic: 1 He is dumb Loads of people “realize” he was just stupid to do so. But the rest have this stance: 2 It was not dumb. In the Bad Batch we see some reasons why the Empire chose to move away from clones. But there are a few more factors: Plus, the Stormtroopers are not meant to be as incompetent as they look. Obi-Wan praises them in ANH so it’s clear the original idea was for them to be skilled fighters.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What was your favorite part of 'Rogue One'? Did anything surprise you about the movie if you have seen it?
Answer: What was a surprise and something I liked is how… [spoiler alert] 3v3ry0n3 d135 I’m not one for dark endings in total, but they are needed for big universes like Star Wars. Not only did this movie have a balance in itself by having the heroes step towards winning the war (while losing the battle) but it also have a great effect overall. When you see the heroes don’t always win, it makes fights tense. You question, “can they make it this time?” That is integral to great storytelling. Real stakes. Rogue One kind of “took one for the team” in the grand scheme of Star Wars. But it was far from bad. It was slow, but kept me engaged the whole time. Honestly, I highly recommend it.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: In the Star Wars universe, can you use the Force to heal yourself?
Answer: Yes, you can indeed. Ki-Adi Mundi Force Heal-ing himself Honestly, I like that. And I think it makes sense. The Jedi during the prequel era are too focused on giving and selflessness regardless of where it comes from. They focus on the fruit, not the root. That’s why Anakin looked like a hero all along (he was almost forced to) while they did not give attention to what was happening inside. Focus on the root, and you get good fruit. Because in the end, that paint goes away, and the fruit falls, showing you what the tree really yields. But the Light Side is root-centric and sharing. Overflowing with life. Not about dying to self, it’s about thriving for others. So, giving up life Force is just not as fitting how I see it.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: When Anakin screamed “I hate you” to Obi Wan, did he truly mean it or was it years of repressed anger towards Obi Wan finally being released?
Answer: Good question. Honestly, he meant it. One of the saddest scenes in cinema Anakin vented at Obi-Wan every now and then. He sometimes felt Kenobi was jealous, but when he was thinking clearly, he saw Obi-Wan for the good brother he was. Anakin didn’t build up hate for Kenobi, Anakin just became consumed by hate because of the Dark Side. It twisted his mind; all he could see was the bad in everyone else. Sadly, Anakin really felt hate for Kenobi, and it was not because of minor things piling up. It was due to how Skywalker chose to fill himself with hate. And Kenobi just objectively sliced Skywalker up, on top of stealing Padme in Anakin’s mind.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How would the fight on Mustafar go if Anakin faced Plo Koon instead of Obi-Wan?
Answer: … not well. Obi-Wan knew Anakin well and was the greatest Soresu practitioner ever. Plo Koon does not know Anakin nearly as well and is ironically also a Djem So practitioner. Second to Skywalker. So, I don’t see this ending well for my boy or the galaxy as a whole.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What were Obi-Wan Kenobi's greatest individual achievements?
Answer: Oh, boy. In Kenobi’s long career, he has not failed to impress. Obi-Wan has gone toe to toe with most of the strongest foes the galaxy had to offer him. Let’s look at his best achievements: (In no particular order) 1 Forcing famed Jedi hunter Jango Fett to retreat Not much to say here. Jango killed Jedi in hand-to-hand combat in Legends. 2 Defeating Maul in TPM Obviously, Qui-Gon took a lot out of Maul with Kenobi and Maul’s arrogance was needed for the win, but the feat is still impressive. Kenobi was the first to defeat a Sith Lord in millennia and cut Maul’s saber in half fair and square (also had him on the floor, nearly dead) as far as Padawan feats go, this is very impressive. 3 Defeating General Grievous Once and for all That guy is one slippery fish. And a hugely infamous Jedi-killing machine. In the novelization, it was said Grievous could dish out 20 strikes per second. (trading out quality for quantity, 16 is rather comfortable for him) many Jedi tried, only one did. 4 Walking out of a 1v2 with Maul and Savage looking better than the duo This is my personal favorite and the one that comes to my mind first. Maul alone is absolutely deadly, but with Savage? That is legendary stuff. Savage alone is also deadly! Walking away from that with only one leg is impressive, but walking away knowing one of the other guys lost an arm is next level. 5 Defeating Knightfall Vader This fight may have come down to a dumb slip up, but we can all agree that the Mustafar duel is a legendary feat for Kenobi. They fought the longest lightsaber duel ever there, proving it was indeed a close match. And we all know Knightfall Vader is no one to mess with. 6 Defeating Darth Vader in Kenobi While we all knew something was a little botched here, it is a Canon feat nonetheless. Beating Darth Vader on his worst day is still crazy, so let’s give Kenobi his flowers. 7 Staying strong! And much more, but just let this meme sink in. I don't think I need to add much. He had so many reasons to fall to the Dark Side, but he didn’t. He stayed a hero, through so much suffering. That is his greatest hachement in my mind. [Most of the art is from Venamis(.com)] I hope you enjoyed, comment which achievements I missed, and have a good one!

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: In the Star Wars universe, what is the actual appeal of becoming a Sith? Are there tangible perks, such as personal wealth, fame, prime real estate etc., or why would anyone voluntary seek to join this despised order?
Answer: Ah, I like this. Most people are like: “I’m sorry, but the Dark Side just is cooler.” You see the cost. Time to mix things up. Are there tangible perks, such as personal wealth, fame, prime real estate etc., or why would anyone voluntary seek to join this despised order? Well, all of what you mentioned is part of the appeal for some Sith like Palpatine. But for most, power is a main hook for the Dark Side. It’s addictive, and George Lucas describes the Dark Side like pleasure. Even though the Light Side has joy and true happiness, the Dark Side feels good. Anakin was drunk on power during RotS, he thought he was more powerful than Palpatine and began thinking of all the possibilities (like ruling the galaxy!) And finally, we have the main part! In the Star Wars universe, what is the actual appeal of becoming a Sith? There’s actually not always an appeal to becoming a Sith, rather the Dark Side always dangles the greatest offer: whatever you want. That’s why the power is wanted, with it, you can get things. Fame, money etc. Look at the Sith Code: I gain, I gain, I gain For anyone who is not happy with their life, for anyone who has a longing or strong want they feel it is needed, the Dark Side is almost irresistible.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How do you feel about the Lego Ninjago Movie?
Answer: Not bad! It’s viewed as garbage and kind of meme, but I’ll give a serious review. First off, relative to the main continuity, it has one big pro and one big con. Negative: it disrespects the canon while many fans wanted it to fit in. Positive: it revived and reformed NINJAGO Overall, I’d actually say modern NINJAGO is near its peak (if not, it has found its new one) And the designs the movie gave are way better than the OG designs (yeah, that’s going in CCO) Now, just looking at it by itself: Negative: I don’t need the characters to match perfectly, but there were two straight up character assassinations. The above is no wisecracking bad@$$, that is a wimp. And the below: Is so bland and boring you’d do the movie a favor by removing the monstrosity. Next, jokes were mid. If it was like the series, I’d say they did okay, but they put this out as a comedy, so I expect slightly more. Positive: The sweet ‘ol “the LEGO movie” animation was fire. And… I know it’s twofaced, but this thing does have some banger jokes. Aside from that, there are two other highlights for me: Relatable setting Making the movie take place in what’s essentially our world was cool because it allowed Lloyd to be like a mirror for a normal kid in school. It led to him having some personal struggles that are supremely relatable. The messages The message on working to improve yourself and struggling to make the best of your inner skills was fantastic, and so was the message on personal value via Lloyd and his leadership role. I found myself walking away with some productive ideas after rewatching it. Honestly, I’d recommend giving it a rewatch if you liked the LEGO movie. It’s very similar.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Would Darth Vader be able to survive if he embraced the light side, and wasn't mortally wounded by Sidious?
Answer: Yes! In what was essentially a Star Wars’ “What If” comic, Vader turned to the Light Side and - as you can see- stayed with the living: When the suit was not working, Vader needed to embrace the Dark Side to live. But whenever it was functioning, he could focus the Force on other things, like crushing rebelscum. There is no evidence for this, but it’s a cool idea that Vader could possibly Force Heal himself fully. I mean, he is the Chosen One and one of the most powerful Force Users ever; who says he can’t even re-grow a limb?

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why does Darth Vader seem so terrifying and sadistic since the third installment of “Obi-Wan Kenobi”? He seems like someone out of a horror movie now and less of a science-fiction character. Has Disney made him too dark now or is this a good arc?
Answer: That’s honestly what Vader is meant to look like (especially the terrifying part) Being realistic, not much can be “too dark” for Vader. He lost his wife after sacrificing everything else he had just to save her. And then he full submerged himself under Palpatine’s rule and the Dark Side. Vader is a monster, that’s what makes him more intimidating and what makes his redemption powerful. He is broken. A tragic character (that’s how George Lucas himself describes Anakin) The only “too dark” comes from the real world, like how Star Wars is meant to be for everyone. Now, there is a line, but personally, I don’t think they crossed it. Nothing was graphic. And we all already saw the infamous “Master Skywalker, there are too many of them” scene. So, all in all, I find Kenobi’s representation of Vader one of the better ones in the Canon.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Did Obi-Wan have to earn a living when he was in exile on Tatooine for those 19 years?
Answer: Yes, otherwise he’d have trouble living. Kenobi riding to/from work Although that was not a bummer. Many people hate working, but not Kenobi. And that’s not because he has a passion for everything, it’s just his character. He wants to be given a task and to do it. Work is simple; it takes his mind off of foul memories and soothes him. What many find “boring” Kenobi finds “calming”. Anakin had a similar thing going on actually: Basic tasks can be a relief. And unlike Anakin, Obi-Wan loves routine, so it probably didn’t get that old.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Did Obi-Wan regret his actions towards Anakin?
Answer: Yes, very much. He felt like he failed Anakin; even said it in RotS In the Kenobi series we see clearly what’s going on in Obi-Wan head concerning regret. Obi-Wan’s sense of guilt is actually at the heart of the story. The series ends when he finally let go and listened to the truth Vader had to offer. “You didn’t kill Anakin, I did” Ultimately, it really was not Obi-Wan’s fault. Palpatine did all he could to turn Anakin, but it was still Skywalker himself who chose the Dark Side.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: In the Star Wars show Obi-Wan, Vader is commanding a small army of Sith (or renegade Jedi, same diff) warriors. Is this a problem for the emperor?
Answer: You’ve likely heard this before, but: Vader is commanding a small army of Sith (or renegade Jedi, same diff) Sith >>>>>> renegade Jedi Sith lords are possibly the deadliest faction in Star Wars. The army of 12 Vader and the Emperor command are called Inquisitors, trained for one purpose: hunting Jedi. Is this a problem for the emperor? Actually, no. For one, Vader obeys the Palpatine. And Vader alone can take on all the Inquisitors. If they teamed on the Emperor, that would be a problem. But he made sure that would not happen. The Inquisitors have extra fancy lightsabers and weaponize intimidation. So, they take down possibly stronger opponents sometimes and also look extra strong. But in reality, they are average Jedi Knight level, if not a bit lower.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Why did Darth Vader lose to Obi-Wan Kenobi? Wasn't he more powerful and should have easily won the fight?
Answer: This Vader? Art by Venamis By RotS, Vader was like a glass Canon. Not in the sense that he was easy to defeat, but in the sense that he was wildly unstable. That is what lead to his bad choice to jump. Wasn't he more powerful and should have easily won the fight? So, is he had all the power he gained through the Dark Side, didn’t spend energy on errands beforehand, and didn’t make some dumb mistake, yes. Anakin would be a clear notch above Kenobi. But that was not the case. Obi-Wan was in his absolute peak (the only moment in his life where he was as formidable is only debatably his prime form in the Kenobi series) Kenobi was focused and as powerful as ever, while Anakin was overrun with emotion and just received loads of power. He overestimated his power (as do most of Kenobi’s opponents when you think about it) Anakin thought he was more powerful than Sidious at the time. So, ultimately, that power was brought down by a poor mental state.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What is the meaning behind Obi-wan's statement "from a certain point of view"?
Answer: I lied to your face, but let’s pretend I didn’t. Okay, okay, not quite. But he led Luke to believe something through deceiving him with careful wording. He’s talking about how “Vader killed Anakin”. When really, “they” are one. Luke felt lied to, and I am with him there; he pretty much was. But I also understand Obi-Wan. He only knew that whatever Luke’s reaction to knowing Vader is his father would be, it would not be pretty.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Did Obi-Wan want to fight Maul in Rebels, and why did he kill Maul so quickly?
Answer: No, but Maul wanted nothing more than to fight, so that was unavoidable. And while Maul was still very formidable, there are a few - in-universe- reasons for his quick defeat: If he has to, he wants it to be quick; he’s not some Sith Lord that enjoys toying (and Maul would be a real threat) Underestimate his opponent. He thought Kenobi was out of shape, out of practice. And Maul thought he was getting in Kenobi’s head: You’re protecting something… no, someone. He said with a grin. When Obi-Wan is angry, he’s off balance (like most Jedi) And Maul has done this to Obi-Wan before (plus, after all Maul did to Kenobi, I’m sure the Sith could not understand how Obi-Wan would not be mad at the first sight of Maul) Carefully exploit weakness. (usually after defending from their strength) Obi-Wan knew Maul was mistaken and felt no anger towards Maul. Kenobi had matured beyond his old self (and was still very much in practice) And he manipulated Maul. Watch the stances: Instant reaction: he is Clone Wars Kenobi, ready for a fight. Next, he is Old Ben; he’s done with the Kenobi of the Clone Wars, he’s put it behind him and grew out of some old weaknesses. And finally, he switches again, for this duel, he is Qui-Gon. He honors his master and could probably guess what Maul would do. Maul went straight for the move that killed Qui-Gon, but Obi-Wan read it like a book, and that was the end of Maul. A few people don’t like this duel, and it’s short, but to me, it is one of the best ever. The art of this speaks to me and I really love it.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: How did Vader lose to Luke?
Answer: The real fight was not physical, but is was the decisive battle. Let’s take a look at the fight without emotions involved: Luke: agility… Vader: strength, speed, durability, stamina, Force power, Force knowledge, versatility, dueling, etc. The reason Darth Vader lost is because Luke was right there and had other advantages. let’s look at their minds and emotions in the duel: Vader: confused, suppressed, miserable, unmotivated Luke: caring, hopeful, understanding, confident! When they were talking without lightsabers ignited, Vader could sense Luke was serious and that he truly knew there was good in Vader. And the Darth began to question what he thought for so many years. How could Luke love Vader when he hates himself? So, yeah, when your dark life’s view is crumbling apart and you're beginning to see the light, it’s a little hard to fight in a duel so tightly related to focus. Luke was determined, focused and even angry for the climax of their duel. But Vader barely even wanted to win, in fact, winning the duel meant losing the last bit of his old self. And there’s another massive thing. Killing Luke meant killing one of the last connections to Padme the galaxy had left. Ultimately, winning was losing for Vader, and he was truly challenged with Luke’s hope.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Was Obi-Wan a force projection in Star Wars: A New Hope?
Answer: He was a Force Ghost! When a Jedi who knows the secret to becoming a Force Ghost dies, that Jedi’s conscience is saved. The Jedi becomes a part of the Cosmic Force and becomes able to manifest his/her self into the world of the living. (Like the Cosmic Force manifests itself as the Living Force) Force Projection is a newer ability only shown in one movie (Canonically as far as I’m aware) When you think about it, these abilities are very similar. As Luke was not just a projection of illusion, he could interact from solar systems away. It’s essentially like manifesting yourself as a Force Ghost without dying beforehand… That comes after.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What are some examples of well-written female protagonists? What makes them strong female characters?
Answer: Oh, dang; no one mentioned Ahsoka? Well, be ready for a long ride, let’s hit it. Firstly, let’s go over how well written she is. Her development was spectacular! She started as a sassy new Padawan most people didn’t like. Not very mature, and she doesn’t question anything. Then she changes for the better (character wise, and design wise, I might add) With Anakin’s training and Ahsoka’s own new experiences in the war, she’s been to a lot of different places and heard a lot of different stories. She becomes far more understanding of the galaxy as a whole and leans respect. All while not losing the charm of occasional cheeky wisecrack. And when the Jedi show what the war has done to them by handing Tano over to the Galactic Republic to literally be given the death penalty, she wakes up to her largest bias. She realizes the Jedi are indeed flawed and truly understands she’s not with the perfect good guys and there are bad guys in the Order (not just that, but as touched on in a previous episode, she also knows the opposition has good people) So, she does some of the finest boss-ing Star Wars has ever seen (largely thanks to Anakin’s training, which she grew so well into because of her incredible resilience) and escapes to investigate for herself. She doesn’t run away, she wants to prove she’s innocent, that’s important. And she eventually finds that her own friend betrayed her, really solidifying the lesson. Finally, when she is accepted back, she refuses. She sees the Order has given her what it could, but now she wants to see an objective view. The Jedi had a view far too narrow, so she had to leave her master. After leaving, she lives on Coruscant as a citizen, leaning the views of the average person. She finds that not only do many other people see the flaws of the Jedi, but many people hate the Jedi unfairly. Now from outside the war she looks at it and fully develops her view of the galaxy and life in it. That is where she matures fully. And then she is called to fight once more. You know that finest boss-ing record she set? Yeah, she’ll do that twice more with fighting Darth Maul himself! Venamis art And the rest of the Mandalorian siege (where she is helping because that’s what heroes do, not because it’s her duty) And then she survives Order 66, something less than 100 Jedi could do out of 20,000 strong. How’s that for strong? She’s one of the most skilled and powerful Jedi in the Canon! And she even goes on in terms of maturity; in Rebels and Ahsoka, we see her as a grown adult. Where he fights Vader (one of the most powerful beings, period) But also her former master. Wiser than ever, and still kicking butt. She ends up being so fantastically balanced. Like half Anakin and half Obi-Wan by the end of it all. And she’s teaching by Rebels! Full circle from Padawan to Master. She’s no longer cocky, she’s just confident as she should be. Now, what makes her strong? Simply the fact she got through that mess! She survived many dangers, and we’ve already learned about her prowess. And also, her resilience. You may not be thinking, “so, she made it through, big whoop, what was so hard?” Well, let’s just see what she lost (comment if I missed something): That enough? She lost her whole life and had to make a new one, how’s that for resilient and strong? Thank you so much for spending you time on my answer:

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What is the cutest thing that your dog does?
Answer: He claws at my legs for me to come down with him so he can lie on my lap. A slightly old picture. My sister’s dog did too sometimes: He occasionally rolls over too, but the above is my favorite cute behavior.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: Whats the best way to read a story, slow burn or straight to the action? Is character development necessary for a good story? And do you like stories where everything builds up to the next sequence or things happen randomly during a normal day?
Answer: Oh, this is nice and loaded. Whats the best way to read a story, slow burn or straight to the action? That’s subjective to your experience reading. Just like consuming other fiction, do you like to watch a series normally or binge? Is character development necessary for a good story? Mostly. Character driven stories need this, and they are what make people like stories, it’s simply speaking to us directly. Plot driven stories can be good, but not nearly as great as character driven ones. And do you like stories where everything builds up to the next sequence or things happen randomly during a normal day? I definitely like a build up. But you can have spontaneous side quests and unseen challenges that take up the chapter like in Percy Jackson. The book needs to build to something, but you still have a lot of freedom to put random, small events things in and still make a good story as a writer.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
Question: What's the saddest MCU scene?
Answer: The other answers are great, but I’m surprised to see the first scene that comes to my mind reading this has been overlooked! The scene where the forgetting spell is cast in No Way Home is really high up there in the saddest scenes list. Partly due to the surrounding scenes: Before this, SEVENTEEN-YEAR-OLD Peter Parker lost his mother figure (he already grew up without his biological mother) And in the cruelest way thanks to the Goblin. That’s building up the sadness. Then after that he decides to no reconnect with MJ and Ned, the only two friends he had through the mess like this: See that sign? Can you imagine being a 17 and also one of the most hated people ever? All he had left was Ned and MJ, and that’s what makes the spell casting scene so sad. It is the center of Peter becoming truly alone. Just a young teen. Completely, utterly alone after having everyone he loved ripped away. And this was voluntary. It’s incredible how selfless Spider-Man is (in so many adaptations) That also adds to it: such bad things happening to such a good kid.

Name: Cade Oosthuizen
